Manual handling remains the single largest cause of injuries to our nursing staff. Sprains and strains are the main types of manual handling injury, and of all injuries to registered nurses,
 40 per cent involved the back, 12 per cent the upper limbs, and 9 per cent the lower limbs. Of injuries to enrolled nurses, 30 per cent were to the back and 17 per cent to the upper limbs.
 Beds were involved in nearly all patient-handling activities where injuries occurred, e.g. repositioning and transferring patients.
 The number of injuries is directly related to the number of people participating in the patient lift; a reduction of 40 per cent is seen during team lifting, as opposed to when the patient is lifted by one person. Very few injuries involved the use of hoists.
The purpose of the notice on manual handling is to remind nursing staff that
attempting solo lifts will likely result in an increased number of incidents.

Palpation is used to assess the depth, width, direction and health – or resilience – of a vein. Assessing a vein by palpation before attempting a venepuncture greatly increases the possibility of success,
 and those allied professionals skilled in phlebotomy often depend more on feel than on sight when determining a vein suitable for venepuncture.
 It’s essential to have the patient contract the muscle of the forearm by opening and closing their fist. This forces blood into the veins, thereby distending them further.
 If a vein still cannot be felt and seen, release the tourniquet and have the client lower his or her arm below the level of the heart. Reapply the tourniquet and tap the vein gently.
 Then remove the tourniquet and place a warmed-moist compress over the intended vein for 10-15 minutes. Doing so helps distend the vein further by filling it with blood.

The memo informs staff that when assessing a vein by palpation it is important to
ensure the vein is filled with plenty of blood.

Insulin therapy involves the subcutaneous injection of insulin to reduce hyperglycaemia and inhibit lipolysis and ketogenesis.
 The insulin pen allows convenient, accurate, and portable insulin delivery. They come prefilled and are disposable when empty.
 Multiple doses are possible with each pen or cartridge holding 300 units. When administering, decide where on the body you will give the injection.
 Be sure to give the injection in a different place each time. You may stay in the same general area but at least 1 inch from the last injection, scars, and naval.
 This rotation of injections prevents lipodystrophy – the thickening (lipohypertrophy) and thinning (lipoatrophy) of the injection areas.

What do the guidelines on the insulin pen tell nursing staff to do?
to alternate the injection site regularly

The positioning of patients involves various positions. Primarily this is done for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, which may include,
 but are not limited to, promoting comfort, restoring body function, preventing deformities, relieving pressure, preventing muscle strain,
 restoring proper respiration and circulation and giving treatment. Health care providers must strive to maintain functional patient body alignment while handling the patient in a safe and responsible fashion to prevent pain or injury.
 It is essential to try to reassure the patient to promote relaxation and cooperation; this also includes covering the body of the patient as much as possible to maintain privacy. All health care providers should obtain assistance if positioning involves heavy or immobile patients.

The purpose of the extract is to inform healthcare providers
of the importance of preserving patient comfort at all times.

The following are points to keep in mind regarding wound irrigation. 
Irrigation should NOT be performed in wounds that are actively bleeding heavily, as irrigation may dislodge any clots that are forming.
Wounds should be irrigated every time you change the dressing AND upon initial assessment, as this will allow you to more fully and accurately assess the wound.
Normal saline is the most frequently used irrigant; however, there is evidence that tap water may result in faster wound healing, provided a clean water source is available. Tap water is also far more cost effective.
Pressure is the key to effective irrigation. Too little pressure will fail to remove surface bacteria, which may lead to wound infection. Too much pressure can force surface bacteria into the wound bed, in addition to damaging delicate granulation tissue. Irrigation pressure should be between 4 and 15 psi.
The memo about wound irrigation aims to
outline the specific process staff should follow.
clarify any misconceptions staff may have.

Most back pain is self-limited and resolves within 4 weeks with analgesics, rest, and relaxation. Management focuses on relief of pain and discomfort,
 activity modification, and patient education. Bed rest is recommended for 1 to 2 days, for a maximum of 4 days and only if pain is severe.
 Other effective nonpharmacologic interventions include the application of superficial heat and spinal manipulation.
 Cognitive-behavioural therapy (e.g., biofeedback), spinal manipulation, physiotherapy, acupuncture, massage, and yoga are all effective nonpharmacologic interventions for treating chronic low back pain but not acute low back pain.
 There is a strong need to alter activity patterns to avoid aggravating the pain. Twisting, bending, lifting, and reaching, all of which stress the back, should be avoided. A gradual return to activities and a program of low-stress aerobic exercise are recommended.

This extract from a handbook encourages those with acute back pain to
include exercise into their daily routine.
adjust the way in which they move.
